--- title: "Spatial and temporal dependence" description: "A held-out site can have a neighbour a few kilometres away in the training data, and a model can score well by knowing the neighbourhood. Holding out whole areas of the map measures what it knows without them." order: 4 categories: [assumptions, spatial-temporal] --- ## Neighbouring sites share what a model misses [Independence of observations](independence-of-observations.qmd) found that visits to one site repeat each other, and that resampling or splitting by site deals with it. Sites are not independent of each other either. Two sites a few kilometres apart share a water mass, a current and a stretch of seabed, and whatever a model's inputs miss there, both sites miss it too. That matters when a model is scored. Cross-validation by site holds out scattered sites, so most held-out sites still have a neighbour among the sites the model was fitted to. A model can then predict a held-out site well by knowing its neighbourhood, without having learnt anything that would carry to an area nobody has surveyed. This page shows how much of a score that can be, and how to measure what a model knows without the neighbours. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Spatial blocks hold out whole areas of the map **Spatial blocks** cut the map into squares and hold out every site in a square together. A held-out site's neighbours in the same square are held out with it, so fewer fitted sites lie around it and its position gives less away. Cross-validation by blocks deals the squares into folds as cross-validation by site deals out sites, and scores the model on each fold in turn. ::: {.diagram} ![Cross-validation by site holds out scattered sites, each with fitted sites close by. Spatial blocks cut the map into squares and hold out every site in a square, so a held-out site's neighbours are held out with it and its nearest fitted site is further away. Blocks test what a model knows about areas it has not seen.](img/spatial-blocks.svg){fig-alt="Two cards showing the same map of 44 sites. Cross-validation by site, hold out scattered sites: seven held-out sites are scattered across the map, each joined by a short dashed line to the nearest site used for fitting, so a held-out site's position alone says a lot about it. Spatial blocks, hold out whole areas: the map is cut into six squares and every site in the top middle square is held out; their neighbours are held out with them and their dashed lines to the nearest fitted site are longer, so position says less about them. A note says blocks test what a model knows about areas it has not seen."} ::: ## Worked example The data, the split by site and the negative binomial model are those of [Count regression](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd). Each training site is also given a **block**: the square of half a degree, about 40 by 55 km, that holds the centre of its stations. Ten-fold cross-validation by site and by block, each repeated three times with different folds, scores the models below. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) |> # the half-degree square holding the centre of each site's stations mutate(block = paste(floor(mean(longitude) / 0.5), floor(mean(latitude) / 0.5)), .by = site_id) by_site <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = site_id, v = 10, repeats = 3) by_block <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = block, v = 10, repeats = 3) curve_recipe <- recipe( abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = train ) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") |> step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE)) prepared <- bake(prep(curve_recipe), new_data = NULL) nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(abundance ~ ., data = prepared) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True) # the half-degree square holding the centre of each site's stations centre = train.groupby("site_id")[["longitude", "latitude"]].transform("mean") train["block"] = (np.floor(centre["longitude"] / 0.5).astype(int).astype(str) + " " + np.floor(centre["latitude"] / 0.5).astype(int).astype(str)) def folds(groups): return [fold for r in range(3) for fold in GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=r) .split(train, groups=groups)] by_site = folds(train["site_id"]) by_block = folds(train["block"]) categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] + categorical def squared(column): return (column, Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)), ]), [column]) curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ squared("depth_m"), squared("temperature_c"), ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) fitted_recipe = curve_recipe.fit(train[predictors]) design = sm.add_constant(pd.DataFrame( fitted_recipe.transform(train[predictors]), columns=fitted_recipe.get_feature_names_out())) nb_fit = sm.NegativeBinomial(train["abundance"], design).fit( method="newton", disp=0) ``` ::: ::: The 120 training sites fall into 20 blocks. ### The negative binomial model's errors form patches on the map For each training site, the animals caught over all its visits are divided by the number the negative binomial model predicted for those visits. A ratio of 2 means the site gave twice what its depth, temperature, seabed and the rest led the model to expect; a ratio of ½ means half. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} site_error <- train |> mutate(predicted = fitted(nb_fit)) |> summarise(longitude = mean(longitude), latitude = mean(latitude), caught = sum(abundance), predicted = sum(predicted), .by = site_id) |> mutate(ratio = caught / predicted) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} train["predicted"] = nb_fit.predict(design) site_error = train.groupby("site_id").agg( longitude=("longitude", "mean"), latitude=("latitude", "mean"), caught=("abundance", "sum"), predicted=("predicted", "sum")) site_error["ratio"] = site_error["caught"] / site_error["predicted"] ``` ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(site_error, aes(longitude, latitude, colour = ratio)) + geom_point(size = 3) + scale_colour_gradient2( transform = "log2", midpoint = 1, limits = c(1 / 4, 4), oob = \(x, range) scales::squish(x, range, only.finite = FALSE), breaks = c(1 / 4, 1 / 2, 1, 2, 4), labels = c("¼", "½", "1", "2", "4"), low = ml_palette[["blue"]], mid = "grey88", high = ml_palette[["vermilion"]] ) + coord_quickmap() + labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude", colour = "Caught ÷\npredicted") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Each training site's catch divided by the catch the negative binomial model predicted for its visits. Vermilion sites gave more than predicted, blue sites less. Each site's ratio is noisy, but sites of one colour gather in patches: more than predicted along the western edge, less through the middle.](spatial-and-temporal-dependence_files/figure-html/fig-errors-1.png){#fig-errors fig-alt='A map with longitude from 140 to 142.5 degrees on the horizontal axis and latitude from 41 to 43 degrees on the vertical, showing 120 training sites as points coloured on a scale from blue, a quarter of the predicted catch, through grey, as predicted, to vermilion, four times the predicted catch. Colours are mixed across the map, but vermilion points gather along the western edge between about 42 and 43 degrees north, and blue points gather in the middle of the map around 141 to 141.7 degrees east and 42 to 42.3 degrees north.' width=1300} ::: ::: ::: Each site's ratio rests on a handful of noisy counts, so the map is speckled. Even so, @fig-errors shows patches: sites along the western edge gave more than the model predicted, and sites through the middle gave less. Errors that gather by area mean the model is missing something that neighbouring sites share. The survey is simulated, so the cause is known. The simulation added a smooth pattern over the map that no input measures: some areas hold more of the species than their depth, temperature and seabed explain, and others less. [Linearity and nonlinearity](linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd) found the same pattern bending the depth curves of the random forest and the GAM. In real data, a patch of errors is a pointer to a missing input, such as a front, a sediment type or a fishing closure, and is worth explaining before it is treated as noise. ### Blocks remove most of what position alone predicts A model given only a station's longitude and latitude can predict a new site only by what the sites around it caught. The negative binomial model's straight lines cannot carve the map into patches, but the random forest of [Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) can. Three forests are scored, one on position, one on the environmental inputs, and one on both, under cross-validation by site and by block. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} input_sets <- list( "Position" = c("longitude", "latitude"), "Environment" = c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season"), "Both" = c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude") ) forest_on <- \(columns) { workflow( recipe(reformulate(columns, "abundance"), data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()), rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("regression") ) } schemes <- list("by site" = by_site, "by block" = by_block) forest_scores <- expand_grid(inputs = names(input_sets), scheme = names(schemes)) |> mutate(score = map2(inputs, scheme, \(i, s) { fit_resamples(forest_on(input_sets[[i]]), schemes[[s]], metrics = metric_set(rsq, rmse)) |> collect_metrics() })) |> unnest(score) |> mutate(.metric = if_else(.metric == "rsq", "R²", "RMSE")) forest_scores |> pivot_wider(id_cols = inputs, names_from = c(.metric, scheme), names_sep = " ", values_from = mean) |> select(inputs, starts_with("R²"), starts_with("RMSE")) |> mutate(across(starts_with("R²"), \(x) round(x, 3)), across(starts_with("RMSE"), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|inputs | R² by site| R² by block| RMSE by site| RMSE by block| |:-----------|----------:|-----------:|------------:|-------------:| |Position | 0.076| 0.027| 4.89| 4.62| |Environment | 0.172| 0.129| 4.65| 4.29| |Both | 0.193| 0.143| 4.53| 4.19|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} input_sets = { "Position": ["longitude", "latitude"], "Environment": predictors, "Both": predictors + ["longitude", "latitude"], } def forest_on(columns): numeric = [c for c in columns if c not in categorical] steps = [("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric)] if any(c in categorical for c in columns): steps.append(("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), [c for c in columns if c in categorical])) return Pipeline([ ("recipe", ColumnTransformer(steps)), ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=1, n_jobs=-1)), ]) def score(columns, splits): rows = [] for fit_rows, held_rows in splits: fitted = forest_on(columns).fit(train.loc[fit_rows, columns], train.loc[fit_rows, "abundance"]) predicted = fitted.predict(train.loc[held_rows, columns]) truth = train.loc[held_rows, "abundance"] rows.append({"R²": np.corrcoef(predicted, truth)[0, 1] ** 2, "RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(truth, predicted)}) return pd.DataFrame(rows).mean() schemes = {"by site": by_site, "by block": by_block} forest_scores = pd.DataFrame({ name: pd.concat({scheme: score(columns, splits) for scheme, splits in schemes.items()}) for name, columns in input_sets.items() }).T forest_scores.columns = [f"{m} {s}" for s, m in forest_scores.columns] forest_scores = forest_scores[["R² by site", "R² by block", "RMSE by site", "RMSE by block"]] forest_scores.round(3).reset_index(names="inputs") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | inputs | R² by site | R² by block | RMSE by site | RMSE by block | |:------------|-------------:|--------------:|---------------:|----------------:| | Position | 0.032 | 0.039 | 4.587 | 4.628 | | Environment | 0.123 | 0.116 | 4.184 | 4.206 | | Both | 0.145 | 0.126 | 4.105 | 4.181 | ::: ::: ::: The forest on position alone reaches an R² of 0.076 under cross-validation by site. It knows nothing about the species' surroundings, only which sites lie nearby, so this score is evidence that neighbouring sites share their catch. Under blocks it falls to 0.027, because a held-out site's neighbours now mostly sit in the same held-out block. The forest on the environment falls too, from 0.172 to 0.129. Depth follows position, as [Linearity and nonlinearity](linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd) found, so part of what looked like knowledge of depth was knowledge of the area. A block also tends to hold conditions that the rest of the map covers thinly, which [Uneven sampling and extrapolation](sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) takes up. Adding position to the environmental inputs raises R² by 0.021 under cross-validation by site, but by only 0.014 under blocks. About 30% of what coordinates seemed to add was knowledge of the neighbours, which an unsurveyed area would not have. Every RMSE is lower under blocks, although every R² is lower too. The blocks' folds hold different mixes of rich and poor sites from the sites' folds, so their RMSEs are on different scales, the trap [Information leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd) met when it compared a random split with a split by site. R², which measures each fold against its own spread, can be compared across the two schemes. ## Cross-validation by site and spatial blocks answer different questions Neither score is the right one in general. Cross-validation by site measures how well a model predicts a new site among those already surveyed, such as an unsampled site between two monitored ones. Blocks measure how well it predicts an area nobody has surveyed, which is what a habitat map of a new region needs. Report the scheme that matches the use, and say which it was. How large to make the blocks is a choice of its own, which [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) makes. ## A forecast is tested only on years after its training data Samples close in time resemble each other as samples close in space do: one year's cold winter, or one month's bloom, touches every station sampled then. The same remedy applies, with one difference. | | In space | In time | | --- | --- | --- | | What is shared | Neighbouring sites' water and seabed | A season's or a year's conditions | | What a split by site leaks | The neighbourhood | The future, when later years train the model | | The honest split | Hold out whole areas | Fit to earlier years, test on later ones | Predicting 2021 from a model fitted to 2022 is not merely optimistic; it can never happen in use. A forecast is scored only by holding out the years after the ones the model was fitted to. [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) builds both kinds of split. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Neighbouring sites share water and seabed, so a model's errors gather in patches on the map. A patch points to something the inputs miss. - Cross-validation by site leaves most held-out sites with a fitted neighbour close by, so a model can score well by knowing the area. - A random forest on longitude and latitude alone scored an R² of 0.076 by site and 0.027 by block. Adding position to the environment looked worth 0.021 by site and 0.014 by block. - **Spatial blocks** hold out whole areas and measure what a model knows about places nobody surveyed. Choose the scheme that matches the model's use. - Compare R², not RMSE, across resampling schemes. In time, test only on years after those the model was fitted to. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Change the blocks from half a degree to a quarter, `/ 0.25` in both places, and rerun. Predict first whether the forest on position should score higher or lower under the smaller blocks. 2. Score the forest on position with `vfold_cv(train, v = 10)`, which deals single stations into folds and so lets a site's other visits train the model. How much higher does position score when a held-out station's own site is in the training data?
